title: The Taxonomy of Touch
hook: Touch is the channel with the fewest words and the strictest rules, and the only one where a reading can never replace asking.
why:
Touch is the oldest channel people have. Before an infant can see clearly or understand a word, it is held, fed, rocked and soothed by touch, and touch remains the most direct way one body can affect another. It can comfort a grieving friend more than any sentence, and it can frighten, humiliate or harm more than any look. No other channel carries such strong rules, and no other channel is so often misread with such serious consequences.

This chapter maps the territory. You will learn the main kinds of touch and why confusing them causes trouble, how a single touch can carry many meanings, how relationships draw maps of where on the body each person may touch, why skin is built to register care, how touch follows lines of power, and why the response to a touch tells you more than the touch itself. It ends with the rule that sets touch apart from everything else in this book: you can read a face or a posture without asking, but you can never read your way to permission to touch. Only a clear yes does that.

teach.h: Touch comes in kinds, and confusing them causes trouble.
teach.p:
In 1974 the psychologist Richard Heslin proposed a way of sorting touch into five broad kinds, arranged roughly by intimacy. Functional and professional touch is the touch of a doctor, a barber, a physiotherapist or a tailor, in which the toucher's role gives permission and the touch serves a task. Social and polite touch is the handshake, the brief tap to get attention, the guiding hand at a doorway. Friendship and warmth includes the pat on the back, the arm round the shoulder, the hug between friends. Love and intimacy is the long embrace, the held hand, the stroke of the hair. Sexual touch is its own category, with its own rules.

The categories overlap, and people disagree about where particular touches belong, but the idea behind them is useful. Many of the worst misunderstandings about touch are category errors: a social touch read as friendship, a friendly touch read as intimate, an intimate touch offered where only a polite one was welcome. A doctor's examination is acceptable because both people understand it as functional. The same touch from someone without that role would be an assault.

Categories also change with setting. A hug that is ordinary between friends in a pub may be unwelcome between the same two people in an office. A hand on the arm that is normal in one family or culture may feel intrusive in another.

So the first question about any touch is not *what does it mean?* but *what kind of touch is this, for these two people, here?* If you cannot answer that confidently, you are already in uncertain territory, and the rest of this chapter suggests how to proceed.
teach.disconfirm: If touches in your circle were almost never misread between kinds, so that a friendly touch was never taken as more and a polite one never as less, the category idea would add little for you. Most people can recall at least one category error, given or received.

teach.h: The same touch can mean many things.
teach.p:
In 1985 Stanley Jones and Elaine Yarbrough asked people to record, as soon as possible after it happened, every time someone touched them over three days: who, where on the body, in what situation, and what the touch seemed to mean. From some fifteen hundred such records they identified a range of meanings, grouped into clusters including warmth and support, playfulness, attempts to control or direct, ritual greetings and departures, touches in the course of a task, and accidents.

The same physical touch appeared in many clusters. A hand on the shoulder could be support for someone upset, a way of getting attention, a request to move, a greeting, a playful nudge or an attempt to assert control. What decided its meaning was not the touch itself but the relationship, the situation, the timing, the pressure and duration, and what was said alongside it.

This is the theme of every chapter in this book, and it applies with special force to touch. There is no dictionary entry for a hand on the shoulder, just as there is none for folded arms. A touch is a move in a relationship, and it means what the relationship and the moment make it mean.

For a reader watching others, the lesson is to read touch in its full context before deciding what it says about two people. For someone deciding whether to touch, it is a warning: the meaning you intend is not necessarily the meaning that arrives. You may offer support and be felt as controlling, or offer warmth and be felt as intrusive.

A touch says what the relationship lets it say, and sometimes more than you meant.
teach.disconfirm: If people in your life consistently understood your touches exactly as you intended them, whatever the relationship and setting, the gap between intended and received meaning would be small for you. Asking one or two of them would tell you whether that is so.

teach.h: Relationships draw maps of permission on the body.
teach.p:
In 2015 Juulia Suvilehto, Lauri Nummenmaa, Robin Dunbar and colleagues asked over thirteen hundred people in Finland, France, Italy, Russia and the United Kingdom to colour in, on outline drawings of the body, where each of a long list of people would be allowed to touch them: a partner, a parent, a sibling, a close friend, an acquaintance, a stranger, and so on.

The maps were strikingly consistent. The closer the emotional bond, the more of the body a person was allowed to touch. Partners could touch almost anywhere. Close family and friends could touch the head, arms, shoulders and back. Acquaintances were mostly limited to the hands and arms, and strangers to the hands alone. The same basic pattern appeared in all five countries, though some cultures allowed more touch overall than others.

These maps explain why some touches feel wrong even when nothing about them is hostile. An acquaintance who touches your face or your waist has used a map that belongs to a closer relationship than the one you have. The discomfort is the feeling of a boundary crossed, the same alarm the chapter on proxemics described, but sharper.

Everyone carries their own map, shaped by family, culture, history and temperament. People who have been hurt may have much smaller maps than average. People raised in physically affectionate families may have larger ones. You cannot see another person's map, and you cannot safely assume it matches yours.

When in doubt, assume the map is smaller than yours, and let the other person widen it if they wish.
teach.disconfirm: If people's maps of where others may touch them did not depend on how close the relationship was, the research described here would be wrong. In your own life, notice whether the touches that felt intrusive came from people further away on the map than the touch implied.
teach.pullQuote: You cannot see another person's map, and you cannot safely assume it matches yours.

teach.h: Skin is built to feel care.
teach.p:
Touch is not only a social signal. The skin has nerve fibres that seem specialised for it. In 2009 Line Löken, Håkan Olausson and colleagues recorded the activity of single nerve fibres in people's arms while stroking the skin at different speeds. A class of slow-conducting fibres, known as C-tactile afferents, responded best to gentle stroking at about the speed of a caress, and the more strongly they fired, the more pleasant people rated the touch. Faster and slower strokes produced less activity and less pleasure.

Touch can also carry specific feelings. In 2006 Matthew Hertenstein, Dacher Keltner and colleagues asked strangers to communicate emotions to each other by touching only the other person's forearm, with a barrier between them so that nothing could be seen. Receivers identified anger, fear, disgust, love, gratitude and sympathy at rates well above chance, from touch alone.

And touch can lighten a load. The chapter on the quiet body in Part VI described a study in which holding a partner's hand reduced the brain's response to the threat of a shock, most of all in the happiest marriages.

All of this explains why touch is so powerful and so risky. The same channel that can soothe with remarkable directness can also intrude with remarkable directness. The nerves that register a welcome caress register an unwelcome one just as clearly, and the feeling that follows is the opposite of comfort.

Touch reaches people more directly than anything else you can do, which is exactly why it requires their agreement.
teach.disconfirm: If gentle touch from a trusted person felt no more pleasant or calming than any other touch, the findings on caress-tuned nerves and stress would not apply to you. Such individual differences exist, which is another reason to ask rather than assume.

teach.p:
In the 1970s the psychologist Nancy Henley observed that touch often flows down hierarchies. Bosses touch employees on the shoulder more than employees touch bosses; doctors touch patients; teachers touch pupils; older people touch younger ones. She argued that the freedom to touch without asking is itself a privilege of status. Later observational research, including work by Judith Hall, found the pattern weaker and more dependent on setting than Henley had proposed, but the asymmetry she noticed is still worth watching for.

The question to ask about any touch between people of unequal power is whether it could easily be refused. A manager who puts a hand on an employee's shoulder during a review, a senior colleague who hugs a junior at a party, a coach who pats a young player: in each case the person being touched may not feel free to step away, object or say no, and their stillness tells you nothing about their wishes.

For a reader, this means watching who touches whom, and whether the touch is returned. Touch that runs only one way between two people is often telling you about the relationship's power, not its warmth. Touch that is returned in kind, at a similar level, is more likely to be mutual.

For someone with power, it means a higher bar. Where you hold authority over someone, choose words instead of touch unless they have clearly invited it, and pay attention to any sign that your touch is being endured rather than welcomed. The chapter on the ethics of reading people makes the same point about readings: the more power you hold, the higher the standard.

The freedom to touch without asking is a privilege. Use it as little as possible.
teach.disconfirm: If touch between people of unequal power in your setting turned out to be returned as often by the junior as by the senior, and refused as easily, the asymmetry would not be operating there. Watch a few such relationships before assuming either way.

teach.h: Read the response, not the touch.
teach.p:
The most informative part of any touch is how the person touched responds. Do they lean into it, relax, return it? Or do they stiffen, go still, shift their weight away, end the conversation, or glance towards someone else? Responses unfold over a second or two, and they are often clearer than anything the toucher intended.

Be especially careful with stillness. A person who does not move away from a touch has not necessarily welcomed it. People often freeze when touched unexpectedly or unwantedly, particularly by someone with power, someone larger, or someone whose reaction they fear. Freezing is a common response to threat, and the chapters of Part II discuss it further. It looks like acceptance from the outside, and it is not.

The response can also change over time. Someone who welcomed a hug a year ago may not welcome one now, after a loss, an illness, an argument or a change in the relationship. Every touch is a new question, and the last answer does not settle the next.

A short word on influence. Some studies have reported that a brief touch on the arm can increase compliance or generosity, for example tips in restaurants, in what was called the Midas touch. The findings are mixed. Either way, touching people in order to influence them is a technique of the kind this book refuses to teach. It uses the most direct channel a body has for a purpose the other person has not agreed to.

Read the response, and take anything short of a clear welcome as a reason to stop.
teach.disconfirm: If people who froze when touched turned out, when asked later, to have welcomed the touch as often as people who leaned into it, stillness would be a weaker warning sign than this block claims. The research on freezing under threat, and many people's accounts, suggest otherwise.

teach.h: Touch is the one channel where you must ask.
teach.p:
Every other chapter in this book teaches you to read without asking, and then to ask when it matters. Touch reverses the order. With touch, reading is never enough. The statement at the front of this book puts it plainly: in touch, closeness and sex, the only signal that grants permission is a clear yes, and no posture overrides a word.

Asking can be simple and light. *Hug?* with open arms that can easily turn into a handshake. *Is it all right if I put my hand on your shoulder?* when someone is upset. A hand offered rather than a hand taken. Waiting for the other person to complete a gesture you have started. The chapter on consent in Part III treats this in depth.

Children deserve the same respect. A child who stiffens and turns away when relatives insist on a goodbye hug is telling you something about their own body, and making them comply teaches them that their body's signals do not count. Offering a wave or a high five instead teaches them the opposite.

Culture, religion and history shape what people will welcome. In some traditions, touch between men and women outside the family is not appropriate at all, and a handshake declined is a matter of faith, not rudeness; Part V discusses this. Men's touch with other men carries its own rules and its own costs, which Part III explores. People who have experienced violence may need much more space than their friends realise.

Read everything else. Ask about touch.
teach.disconfirm: If asking before touching made people consistently less comfortable than touching without asking, by their own account, the rule would cost more than it protects. Most people, asked, say they prefer being asked, and the cost of a wrong guess is far higher than the cost of a question.

caseStudy:
Dan, forty-two, coaches an under-twelves football team on Saturday mornings. He grew up in a family that hugged and slapped backs, and he coaches the same way: a pat on the back after a good pass, a hand on the shoulder when explaining a drill, a ruffle of the hair after a goal. Most of the boys seem to like it.

In his second season a new boy, Kai, joins the team. After Kai scores in his first match, Dan claps him on the back. Kai flinches, his shoulders jump up, and he steps sideways out from under the hand. He says nothing and runs back to his position. Dan notices it and, for once, does not do it again.

Over the next few weeks he watches more carefully, not only Kai but the whole team. He notices that two other boys also go still when patted, smiling politely but holding their arms tight to their sides. He had been reading their stillness as acceptance. He also notices that several boys initiate contact themselves: they run up for a high five, or bump his fist.

Dan changes his habit. He offers a raised hand for a high five or a fist bump and lets each boy choose whether to complete it. He explains drills with words and demonstrations instead of steering boys by the shoulders. When a boy is upset, he crouches beside him and asks what happened, rather than putting an arm round him straight away.

Kai's mother mentions at the end of the season that Kai has sensory sensitivities and that unexpected touch is genuinely painful for him. She thanks Dan for the high fives. Kai, she says, likes being able to decide. Dan realises that the boys who used to go still were telling him the same thing, and that most of them now choose the fist bump.
observe: In a public place, notice touches between people you can see, and for each ask what kind of touch it was and how the person touched responded.
Notice who touches whom in a workplace or family gathering, and whether the touches are returned at the same level.
The next time you touch someone, even briefly, watch their response for the following two seconds.

drills.name: Touch Diary
steps: For two days, write down every time someone touches you or you touch someone, as soon as you can afterwards.
For each, note who, where on the body, the situation, and what kind of touch it was.
Note what you think the touch meant, and how it felt.
Mark any touch that felt like a different kind from the one intended.
At the end, write one pattern you notice in your own touching.
variations: Extend the diary to a week, and note how the touches you receive differ between workdays and weekends.
Add a column for touch you wanted and did not get, or offered and was declined.
Ask a partner or close friend to keep the diary on the same days, and compare what each of you noticed.

drills.name: Your Own Map
steps: Draw a simple outline of a body, front and back.
For three people, a close friend, a colleague and an acquaintance, shade where each could touch you comfortably.
Compare the three maps.
Think of one person whose touch has felt intrusive, and mark where it fell on the map for your relationship.
Write down what that tells you about maps that differ from yours.
variations: Draw a fourth map for a person whose authority you are under, such as a manager or doctor, and compare it with the others.
Draw the maps you think two other people hold for you, and if you dare, ask one of them how close you came.

drills.name: Response Watch
steps: Over a week, watch for touches between other people in public places, in films or in your workplace.
For each, note the response of the person touched in the following two seconds.
Sort the responses into welcoming, neutral, stiffening or freezing, and moving away.
Note any case where the toucher did not seem to notice the response.
Write one sentence about what you would have done in the toucher's place.
variations: Watch at a station or airport arrivals area, where greetings and partings are frequent and varied.
Focus on parents and children for one session, noticing which touches children seek and which they avoid.

drills.name: Ask Lightly
steps: Choose two or three moments this week when you would normally touch someone without thinking, such as a greeting or comfort.
Instead, offer the touch in a way that can be declined, such as an open hand or a light question.
Notice how the other person responds, and whether they complete the gesture.
Note how asking felt to you.
Write down one way of asking that felt natural enough to keep.
variations: Try asking in words with someone you would normally touch without thinking, and notice their reaction to being asked.
Practise the open-arms offer that can turn into a handshake, and notice how often people choose each.

drills.name: Power Check
steps: List the people over whom you hold some authority, such as staff, pupils, players or younger relatives.
For each, note whether you touch them, how, and whether they touch you in return.
Mark any touch that runs only one way.
For each marked touch, consider whether the person could easily refuse it.
Decide which touches you will replace with words or with gestures they can choose to complete.
variations: Ask one person in the group how they feel about the touch that runs one way, if you can do so without pressure.
Review the list again in three months and note which touches you have dropped, which you kept, and how people responded.

quiz.q: A colleague did not pull away when you put your arm round her shoulders at a party. What does that tell you?
options: That she welcomed it, since she would have moved away if she had not
That she is interested in you and would welcome more closeness later
Very little: stillness may be freezing or politeness, not consent
That the touch was appropriate for that setting and that relationship
quiz.explain: People often go still when touched unexpectedly or unwantedly, especially at work or by someone with power. Stillness is not consent. Only a clear welcome or a clear yes tells you a touch was wanted.

quiz.q: What did Suvilehto and colleagues' body maps of permitted touch show across five countries?
options: The closer the bond, the more of the body that person was allowed to touch
People allowed strangers and partners to touch them in almost the same places
Each country produced a completely different map with no shared pattern at all
People allowed touch only on the hands, whatever the relationship involved
quiz.explain: Partners could touch almost anywhere, close family and friends the upper body, acquaintances mostly the arms and hands, strangers the hands alone. The pattern was shared across countries, with differences in how much touch each allowed.

quiz.q: What did Löken and colleagues find about C-tactile nerve fibres in the skin?
options: They respond most strongly to sharp, sudden pain anywhere on the body
They respond only to changes in temperature, not to any kind of pressure
They are found only in the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet
They respond best to slow, gentle stroking, which people find pleasant
quiz.explain: These fibres fired most at caress-like speeds, and their activity tracked how pleasant the touch felt. Skin seems built to register care, which makes unwanted touch as direct as welcome touch.

quiz.q: Your young nephew stiffens and turns away when relatives insist on a goodbye hug. What fits this chapter?
options: Insist on the hug, since it is rude to refuse relatives who love him
Let him choose another goodbye, such as a wave or a high five
Ignore it, since children always dislike hugs at that age anyway
Explain to him afterwards why relatives' feelings must come first
quiz.explain: His body is telling you what he does not want, and making him comply teaches him that his signals do not count. Offering a goodbye he can choose respects him and still lets him say goodbye.

quiz.q: In Hertenstein and colleagues' study, what could strangers communicate by touching only each other's forearm?
options: Nothing beyond whether the toucher was being friendly or unfriendly
Only pleasure and pain, and none of the more specific feelings tested
Several distinct feelings, such as gratitude, sympathy and anger
Only feelings that had first been agreed between them in advance
quiz.explain: Receivers identified anger, fear, disgust, love, gratitude and sympathy from touch alone, well above chance. Touch carries specific meaning, which is why its effects are so direct.

quiz.q: A friend's partner rests a hand on your arm for a long moment while talking with you at a party. What fits this chapter?
options: Note it in context and relationship, and do not take it as an invitation
Take it as a sign of attraction, and return the touch to show you noticed
Mention it quietly to your friend afterwards, in case it meant something
Move away sharply so that nobody could misunderstand what had happened
quiz.explain: A touch means what the relationship and setting make it mean, and many people touch the arm when talking. It does not grant permission for anything. If you are uncomfortable, a gentle step back is enough.

quiz.q: In Jones and Yarbrough's study of touches recorded in daily life, what did they find about the meaning of a given touch?
options: Each kind of touch, such as a hand on the shoulder, carried one fixed and reliable meaning
The same physical touch could carry many different meanings, depending on its context
Touches between strangers carried more meaning than touches between people who knew each other
Most touches recorded were accidental and carried no social meaning for either person at all
quiz.explain: A hand on the shoulder could mean support, attention-getting, control or playfulness, depending on who did it, where and why. That is why touch cannot be read like a dictionary.

quiz.q: A colleague touches your arm several times while talking to you at a work party. A friend says this shows she is attracted to you. What does this chapter suggest?
options: Your friend is right, since repeated touching of the arm is a reliable sign of romantic interest
It shows that she is drunk, since sober colleagues never touch each other at work functions
It carries many possible meanings, and if interest matters to you, only words can settle it
It is an attempt to dominate you, since touch always flows from higher to lower status people
quiz.explain: The same touch can carry warmth, emphasis, habit or playfulness, as Jones and Yarbrough found, and some people touch everyone while they talk. No touch grants or signals permission the way a clear yes does.

quiz.q: What did Nancy Henley propose about touch and status?
options: That people of lower status touch those of higher status more, as a way of gaining favour
That status has no bearing on touch, which depends entirely on friendship and liking
That only touch between equals carries meaning, since unequal touch is always ritual
That touch tends to flow down hierarchies, with higher-status people touching more freely
quiz.explain: Henley argued that the freedom to touch without asking is a privilege of status. Later research found the pattern weaker and more varied, but it is a good reason for caution wherever you hold power over someone.

quiz.q: You have just given a junior colleague difficult news, and he is close to tears. What fits this chapter best?
options: Stay seated, slow down, offer water and time, and say the supportive words without touching him
Put a hand on his shoulder and keep it there, so that he knows you are on his side through it
Hug him, since a hug is the clearest way to show that the news is not personal and you care
End the meeting at once, since showing emotion at work will embarrass both of you if it continues
quiz.explain: Where power runs one way, the person touched cannot easily refuse, and stillness can look like welcome. Words, time and small practical kindnesses carry warmth without asking anything of his body.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific touch you gave or received in the past year that was misread, by you or by the other person. Describe it: who, where on the body, the setting, and what was intended. What kind of touch did each of you take it to be? How did the person touched respond in the moments afterwards, and did anyone notice? What would you do differently now, and how would you ask?
reflection.guidance: Many people find their example at a party, a farewell or a moment of comfort, where kinds of touch blur. Try to separate what was intended from what was received, and notice whether the response was read at the time. The last question matters most. Find a way of asking that sounds like you, light enough to use without making a moment awkward.

failureMode: The commonest failure is to read stillness as permission, mistaking a person's freezing or politeness for welcome. The second is the category error: offering a friendly or intimate touch where only a polite one was invited. The third is to use touch where you hold power, so that the person touched cannot easily refuse, and then to read their compliance as warmth. The fourth is to use touch as a technique to influence people, which this book refuses to teach. And the deepest failure is to apply to touch the method that works for every other channel, reading first and acting on the reading. With touch, reading is never enough. Ask lightly, accept any answer, and let the other person lead.

moreCases.title: The hug at the leaving party
moreCases.scene:
Rob, forty, is leaving the engineering firm where he has worked for eleven years, and at his leaving drinks he goes round the room saying goodbye. He is a hugger. He hugs his manager, the two men he shared an office with, the receptionist he has joked with every morning for a decade. Most of them hug him back, some clumsily, some warmly.

When he gets to Aisha, a project manager he has worked with for two years, she holds out her hand. Rob, a little drunk and full of feeling, says, "Oh, come here," pushes her hand aside and pulls her into a hug. Aisha goes completely still. Her arms stay at her sides. After a second or two Rob lets go, says something warm about how much he will miss her, and moves on to the next person.

Two days later, a friend who is still at the firm tells Rob that Aisha was upset. She had not wanted to make a scene at his leaving party, but she had felt grabbed. She is religious and does not hug men outside her family, which most of the office knew. Rob is mortified. He had thought the hug was a kindness, and since she had not pulled away, he had assumed it was fine.

When Rob thinks back, he remembers that Aisha had held out her hand to him at the start of the party too, when he arrived, and that he had shaken it without thinking. He had simply forgotten, in the warmth of saying goodbye, that he already knew what she offered.

Aisha, for her part, had not wanted to make Rob feel bad on his last day. She had smiled at him afterwards and wished him luck, which made it even harder for him to see that anything had gone wrong.
moreCases.misread:
Rob read Aisha's stillness as acceptance. Because she did not push him off, he assumed she did not mind. He had also overridden the clearest possible signal, an offered hand, which told him exactly what kind of touch she was willing to give.

And because she said nothing at the time, Rob had no chance to notice his mistake until it had already travelled round the office.

The drink and the emotion of the evening lowered the half-second of attention that might have caught it, which is worth remembering at every party where goodbyes are said.
moreCases.betterRead:
The offered hand was the reading, and it needed no interpretation: a handshake was the touch on offer, and matching it was the whole of good manners. The stillness that followed was not consent but a common response to an unwanted touch, especially in public, especially from someone the person likes and does not want to embarrass. People freeze far more often than they push away. The rule this chapter teaches is simple: match the touch that is offered, and when you want to offer more, offer it in a way that can be declined, such as open arms that can turn into a handshake, and then watch what the other person chooses. Rob wrote to Aisha to apologise, without excuses. She replied kindly. He has stopped pulling people into hugs.

Many people find it helps to make the offer explicit when there is any doubt: a quick "handshake or hug?" with a smile is light enough to be friendly and clear enough to give the other person the choice.

moreCases.title: The hand on the shoulder in the appraisal
moreCases.scene:
Ian manages a team of twelve in a housing association. In an annual review, he has to tell Jordan, twenty-four, that his performance has not been good enough and that he will be put on an improvement plan. Jordan takes it badly. His eyes fill, he looks at the floor, and his voice cracks when he says he understands.

Ian, who is a kind man, gets up, comes round the desk, and puts his hand on Jordan's shoulder, leaving it there while he says that he believes in him and that they will work through this together. Jordan stays completely still under the hand. He says thank you. When Ian sits back down, Jordan wipes his eyes and leaves as soon as he can.

Months later, after Jordan has moved to another team, he tells a colleague that the review was one of the worst moments of his working life, and that the hand on his shoulder made it worse. He had felt pinned, he says, unable to move away from the man who had just told him he was failing, and expected to be grateful.

Ian, for his part, remembers the review as difficult but handled well. He thinks the hand on the shoulder was one of the kinder things he did that day. Nobody has ever told him otherwise.
moreCases.misread:
Ian read the moment as a call for comfort and offered the touch he would offer a friend. He took Jordan's stillness and his thanks as signs that the comfort was welcome. He did not notice that he was the one person in the building Jordan could not refuse.

Jordan's thanks were part of the same pattern: a junior employee, upset, in his manager's office, saying the polite thing. Ian took the words as evidence that the touch had helped.

Ian also assumed that what comforts him would comfort Jordan. Many people in distress want, above all, to be left a little space to collect themselves, and a hand on the shoulder takes that space away.
moreCases.betterRead:
Henley's observation that touch tends to flow down hierarchies matters most in exactly these moments. A manager who touches a junior, a doctor who touches a patient, a coach who touches a player, is offering something the other person cannot easily decline, and compliance looks very like welcome. The careful response to Jordan's distress was to stay in his seat, slow down, offer a tissue and a glass of water, say the same supportive words, and give Jordan time and the option to finish the conversation later. Words can carry warmth without asking anything of the body. Where power runs one way, they are usually the kinder choice.

If Ian had wanted to offer something physical, a tissue box slid across the desk, or a door held open at the end, would have carried the same care without the weight.

The same holds for teachers with pupils, coaches with players, doctors with patients and officers with members of the public. The more authority you hold, the more carefully your touch should be offered, and the more readily you should choose words instead.

moreCases.title: The father who stopped hugging
moreCases.scene:
Steve hugged his son, Callum, every night until Callum was about twelve. Then, around the time Callum started secondary school, Steve noticed his son stiffening slightly when he went in for a hug in front of friends, and once Callum said, "Dad, not here." Steve took the hint, and more than took it. He stopped hugging Callum altogether, at home as well as in public. He thought he was respecting his son's wishes.

Callum is now sixteen. One evening, after a bad day in which he has fallen out with his closest friend, he sits on the stairs with his head in his hands. Steve finds him there, stands at the bottom of the stairs, asks if he is all right, gets a muttered answer, and goes back to the kitchen. Later, Callum's mother, who has stayed closer to him, tells Steve that Callum said he wished his dad still hugged him. He had thought, she says, that his father had decided he was too old for it.

Steve, when his wife tells him, is stunned. He had thought he was doing his son a kindness by stepping back. It had never occurred to him that Callum might be waiting for him to step forward again.
moreCases.misread:
Steve read one specific signal, embarrassment at being hugged in front of friends, as a general withdrawal of permission. He then stopped offering touch altogether, which Callum read, in turn, as his father pulling away. Each misread the other, and the misreadings fed each other for four years.

Neither of them ever said any of this aloud. Each simply adjusted to what he thought the other wanted, and the distance grew by small steps that both of them took for respect.

Steve also missed the most important part of Callum's sentence. "Not here" carries its own exception: somewhere else would be fine.

Both loved each other throughout.
moreCases.betterRead:
Suvilehto's body maps found that close family are allowed to touch large parts of the body, but the form and setting of that touch change as children grow. A teenager's "not here" is usually about the audience, not about the touch itself. The careful reading keeps offering, in forms the son can accept or decline: a hand on the shoulder in passing, sitting next to him on the stairs, an arm briefly round him at home, asked for lightly. Steve sat down on the stairs beside Callum the following week, after another bad evening, and put an arm around his shoulders. Callum leaned into it, and they sat there for a long time without saying much.

It is worth noticing how much four years of silence had cost them both, and how little it took to end it: one father sitting down on one stair, and one arm offered rather than imposed.

moreCases.title: The physiotherapist who narrates
moreCases.scene:
Gareth, fifty-five, has a knee replaced after years of pain, and begins physiotherapy two weeks later. His first physiotherapist works quickly and efficiently, moving his leg into positions, pressing around the scar, holding his ankle to bend the knee. Gareth tenses at every touch, flinches twice, and finds that his knee bends less each session rather than more. The physiotherapist notes that he is guarding the joint and tells him to relax.

When that physiotherapist goes on leave, Gareth is seen by another, Nadia. Before she touches him, she tells him what she is going to do and where: she is going to put one hand under his calf and one above the knee, and gently bend it until he says stop. She asks him to say stop. She narrates every movement, and pauses whenever his breath catches. In that first session, Gareth's knee bends further than it has since the operation. He tells her, at the end, that he had been dreading the sessions, and that he had not realised how much of the dread was about being handled without warning.

Nadia tells him that this is common, and that many patients, men especially, never say that the touching is part of the problem. They just tense, and are told to relax, and tense more.

The first physiotherapist was not careless; she was busy, skilled and used to patients who wanted her to get on with it. What she had not had was a patient who told her that the touching itself was hard.
moreCases.misread:
The first physiotherapist read Gareth's tension as a problem of the knee, guarding a painful joint, and treated it with an instruction to relax. She did not consider that the tension might be partly a response to the touch itself: unannounced, firm, from a stranger, on a body in pain.

Telling a tense patient to relax rarely works; it adds an instruction to the tension. What helps is changing whatever is causing it.

Gareth, for his part, had never thought to say anything. He assumed the flinching was just part of recovering from an operation, and that a tougher man would not have done it.
moreCases.betterRead:
Functional, professional touch, the first of Heslin's kinds, is permitted by the role, but the role does not remove the body's response to being touched without warning. Many people, and particularly people who have been hurt in the past, tense or freeze when touched unexpectedly, even by someone they trust. Narrating touch before it happens turns it from something done to the person into something agreed with them, and giving them a word to stop it gives them back control. Gareth's knee had not been the problem. The lack of warning had.

The same principle applies far beyond physiotherapy: barbers, dentists, nurses, tailors and carers all touch people for a task, and all of them can make that touch easier by saying what comes next.

workedReading.title: At the funeral
workedReading.scene:
Your friend Sam's father has died. At the funeral, after the service, Sam is standing near the door of the church, greeting people. He is shaking hands, nodding, saying thank you. His face is set and his voice is steady. When you reach him, he looks at you, and something in his face gives way for a moment; his eyes fill and his jaw tightens. He holds out his hand.

You have travelled two hours to be there. You have not seen Sam since his father became ill, and you are not sure how he is coping. The queue behind you is long, and his mother is standing beside him.

Sam's father was a quiet, reserved man who shook hands with his own sons, and Sam has always been more like him than he likes to admit. You have hugged Sam perhaps three times in twenty years, all of them at weddings, all of them after a few drinks.

steps.label: Check yourself
steps.text:
You want to hug him. You have known him for twenty years, and you feel the grief of the moment yourself. That wish is real and kind, and it is also yours. Before acting on it, you notice that it is your impulse, and that the question is what Sam wants, here, with a queue of people behind you.

Grief at funerals is contagious, and it is easy to act on your own feeling and call it comfort. Naming the impulse as yours keeps it from making the decision on its own.

steps.label: Read what is offered
steps.text:
Sam has held out his hand. That is the touch on offer. It may be all he can manage in public, it may be the form he has been using with everyone to get through the afternoon, or it may be exactly what he wants. Whatever the reason, the hand is the clearest signal you have, and you start by taking it.

A hand held out at a funeral is often a way of getting through: a ritual that keeps the person upright when anything more might undo them. Respecting it respects the work they are doing.

steps.label: Offer more, easy to decline
steps.text:
As you take his hand, you put your other hand lightly over it, which is warmer than a handshake and still entirely within it. You say his name. You leave a beat in which he could pull you in, or let go, or hold on. This is the touch equivalent of an open question: it offers closeness without imposing it.

This is the same principle as the open arms that can become a handshake: the offer is real, and the choice stays with him.

steps.label: Watch the response
steps.text:
Sam's grip tightens. Then he steps forward and puts his other arm around your back, and you hug, briefly and hard. His body is leaning into it, not stiff, and when he steps back his face is wet but less set. The response is clear: he wanted it, and he chose it. If he had held still, or let go at once, that would have been just as clear in the other direction.

Reading the response does not stop once the touch begins. If he had stiffened halfway through, you would have eased off, whatever he had chosen a second earlier.

steps.label: Let him end it
steps.text:
You let him decide when the hug ends, and you step back as soon as he does. With a queue behind you and his composure to keep, he may need it to be short. You say one sentence, that you are so sorry and that you will ring him next week, and move on so that he can carry on greeting people.

Ending a hug is one of the most overlooked parts of touch. Someone who has to wait for you to let go has lost a little of the choice they made.

steps.label: Follow up later
steps.text:
The touch that matters most may come later, away from the crowd. At the wake, you find Sam alone for a moment in the garden, and stand beside him. You do not touch him at first. After a while you put a hand on his shoulder, and he puts his hand over it. Side by side, a hand on the shoulder is easy to shrug off, which is part of why it is so often welcome.

The garden moment also shows that permission can change through a day. A man who needed a handshake at the door may want a hand on his shoulder an hour later, when nobody is watching.

steps.label: What you learned
steps.text:
Sam told you months later that he had shaken hands with a hundred people that day and remembered almost none of them, but that he remembered the hug at the door and the hand in the garden. He also said that two people had hugged him without warning during the afternoon, and that he had not minded, but had felt it was for them more than for him. The difference was the offer.

He also said he had noticed that you let go first, and that it had made the hug feel safe.

It is worth remembering that the same afternoon included both kinds of touch, and that what made the difference was not how much you touched him but whether he had chosen it.

moreFailures.title: The touch as a test
moreFailures.body:
Dating advice sometimes recommends touching someone lightly, apparently by accident, to see how they respond and so to test their interest. A hand that brushes an arm, a knee that touches a knee, a hand on the small of the back to guide them through a door. This book refuses that advice. It treats the other person's body as a testing ground for your hopes, it relies on their politeness and their tendency to freeze, and it moves the burden of saying no onto them. Part III's chapter on attraction and hard limits explains what can honestly be read, and the chapter on consent explains why only a clear yes grants permission. If you want to know whether someone would like you to touch them, the only reliable method is to ask, and to accept the answer.

It also does not work very well. People who are touched in this way often feel uneasy without knowing why, and the unease attaches itself to the person who touched them.

A man who catches himself planning such a touch should ask what he would do with what he learned. If the honest answer is that he would press on until she objected, the test is not about her at all.

moreFailures.title: Touching on autopilot
moreFailures.body:
Some men touch by habit: a slap on the back for every man, a hug for every woman, a hand on every arm while talking. Usually it comes from a warm family or a warm culture, and usually it is kindly meant. But a habit does not check who is in front of it. It reaches the colleague who does not hug, the friend with a sore shoulder, the acquaintance who has been assaulted, the person whose faith or culture asks for distance. If you are a natural toucher, you need not become cold. You need only put a half-second of attention between the impulse and the touch: who is this, what have they offered before, and what are they offering now?

A simple habit helps: before you touch anyone outside your family, notice what they did the last time you met. That memory is usually all the information you need.

moreFailures.title: Withholding all touch out of fear
moreFailures.body:
The opposite failure is quieter and just as common among men. Worried about being misread, about rules at work, about how their touch might be received, some men stop touching anyone except a partner. They stop hugging their children as they grow up, stand at a distance from grieving friends, shake hands with brothers. The result is a great deal of unoffered comfort, and, for many men, a kind of touch hunger they do not have words for. The answer to the risks of touch is not to abandon it. It is to ask, to offer in ways that can be declined, and to read the response. Asking keeps the warmth and removes the danger.

Fathers, in particular, often step back from touch with their sons at exactly the age when the sons most need to know that their fathers have not stepped back from them.

moreFailures.title: Reading a culture's touch as personal
moreFailures.body:
In some cultures men friends hold hands, colleagues kiss on the cheek, and hosts guide guests with a hand on the arm. In others, touch between unrelated people is rare and carefully limited. A man from a high-touch culture may seem forward in a low-touch one; a man from a low-touch culture may seem cold in a high-touch one. Neither is a statement about the person he is with. Part V's chapters on culture and on religion and touch go into this in detail. The working rule is the same as for distance: let the other person show you their norm, match it, and do not take a difference in habit as a message about how they feel about you.

It also cuts both ways: if you come from a low-touch background, a colleague's hand on your arm may feel forward when it is simply how she talks.

And a single person may change: a friend who has lived abroad may come back with a different sense of touch, and someone recovering from illness may want less of it for a while.

questions.q: How can I tell whether a hug would be welcome?
questions.a:
Look first at what is offered. If someone holds out a hand, a handshake is the touch on offer. If they open their arms, a hug is. If you want to offer a hug, open your arms in a way that can easily become a handshake if the other person reaches for your hand instead, and watch which they choose. With people you know well, a light question works: "Hug?" Once a hug starts, notice whether the other person leans in, puts their arms round you and relaxes, or stays still with their arms at their sides. Stillness is not a yes. And let them end it; the person who wants to stop should never have to wriggle free.

With people you know well, it is also worth remembering that the answer can change from day to day. A friend who loves a hug may not want one when he has just had bad news, or when his back is sore.

If you are not sure whether someone ended a hug because they wanted to or because they felt they had to, notice what they do next time you meet. People who welcomed a hug usually offer the next one more readily.

questions.q: Is it ever all right to touch a colleague?
questions.a:
Handshakes, where they are the custom, are fine. Brief functional touch, such as passing something or tapping a shoulder to get attention in a noisy room, usually is. Beyond that, follow the other person's lead, and be most careful where you hold authority over them, because they cannot easily refuse you. Many workplaces have policies that are stricter than this, and they are worth knowing. A useful test is whether the touch would be welcome if they were your manager doing it to you. If in doubt, use words. They carry warmth, praise and sympathy perfectly well without putting the other person's body in an awkward position.

If you are the junior person and a senior colleague's touch makes you uncomfortable, you are entitled to say so, or to step back, and many organisations have someone you can talk to if saying so directly feels risky.

Remember, too, that what feels like harmless warmth to you may sit differently with someone who has had unwanted touch at work before. You cannot know who has, which is a good reason to let them lead.

questions.q: How should I touch my children as they grow up?
questions.a:
Keep offering, and let them choose the form. Young children often welcome a great deal of touch. As they grow, many become self-conscious about it in public, especially in front of their friends, and some go through phases of wanting very little. That is usually about the setting and the age, not about the relationship. Teenagers often still welcome touch at home, in private, in forms that are easy to accept: a hand on the shoulder in passing, sitting close on the sofa, a quick hug at the door. Ask lightly, accept a no without sulking, and offer again another day. Children who are taught that they can decline touch are also learning something vital about their bodies and other people.

Fathers sometimes worry that touching sons will make them soft. Research on male friendship in Part III suggests the opposite: men who grow up with affectionate touch from their fathers tend to find closeness with friends easier, not harder.

If your child declines a hug, say something like, "Fair enough, I'm here if you change your mind," and mean it. A no that is received calmly makes the next yes easier.

questions.q: Why do some people dislike being touched?
questions.a:
For many reasons, most of them nothing to do with you. Some people are sensitive to touch as a sensation, including many autistic people, for whom light or unexpected touch can be genuinely unpleasant. Some have experienced abuse or assault, and touch, especially unexpected touch, can bring that back. Some grew up in families or cultures where touch was rare, or where it was used to control them. Some are in pain, from injury, illness or conditions such as fibromyalgia. Some simply prefer less. None of these needs explaining to you. If someone does not want to be touched, or not in a particular way, the respectful response is to accept it without comment.

If someone you care about dislikes touch, it is worth finding out what they do like. Some people who dislike hugs welcome a hand on the arm, or simply sitting close.

It is also worth knowing that preferences can change with circumstances: after an operation, during illness, during grief, or after a frightening experience. A friend who used to hug may need space for a while, and will usually tell you when that passes.

questions.q: What is the right way to comfort someone who is grieving?
questions.a:
Often presence matters more than touch, and words matter less than people fear. If you know the person well, touch is often welcome: a hug, a hand on the shoulder, sitting close. But grief can also make people want distance, especially in public, and it can make touch from certain people unbearable. Offer, in a way that can be declined, and read the response, as the worked reading in this chapter describes. Side-by-side touch, a hand on the shoulder or an arm round someone as you both look at something else, is often easier to accept than a face-to-face hug. And remember the weeks after, when the crowds have gone and touch is rarer.

If you are unsure, saying something like, "I'm here, do you want a hug or would you rather not?" is rarely wrong, even at a funeral.

Men often find this harder than women, partly because so many grew up with fewer models of comforting touch between men. The side-by-side hand on the shoulder, which many men find easy to give and to receive, is a good place to start.

questions.q: Can touch really carry specific emotions?
questions.a:
More than you might think. Matthew Hertenstein and his colleagues asked strangers to communicate emotions to each other by touching only the other person's forearm, which the receiver could not see. Receivers identified emotions such as anger, fear, disgust, love, gratitude and sympathy at rates well above chance, through differences in the type, pressure and duration of touch. That does not mean touch is a code you can read reliably in daily life; context, relationship and culture all shape what a touch means. But it does mean that touch is a channel in its own right, and that how you touch someone, how firmly, how long, how still, carries as much as whether you touch them at all.

It also suggests that a hurried, distracted touch carries less than people think. If you are going to touch someone to comfort them, slow down and mean it.

watch.title: Dacher Keltner on the importance of physical contact
watch.notice: The psychologist Dacher Keltner on what touch communicates and why it matters. Notice the kinds of touch he describes and the relationships each one belongs to.

reviewPrompt: This week, offer one touch in a way that can be declined, and watch the response for two seconds afterwards.
